paragraphs: Learning an image distribution from image statistics involves an ambiguity: many different images can produce the same statistics. This paper accounts for that multiplicity through a phase space factor. The factor helps explain how statistical descriptions relate to probabilities over images and why the potentials used in Gibbs distributions are not uniquely determined by the statistics alone.

The authors use this perspective to clarify Minimax Entropy learning and derive a faster approximation called Minutemax. The speedup depends on being able to approximate the phase factor with an analytic distribution. In their illustration, a Gaussian approximation produces results close to the earlier Minimax Entropy results they discuss, using only seconds of CPU time.

The analysis also suggests that phase space substantially influences the shape of potentials across image scales. Finally, the authors prove that learning distributions solely in feature space is equivalent to Minimax Entropy learning with a multinomial approximation to the phase factor. This connects an apparently separate modeling approach to a specific approximation within their framework.
neurips-1998-a-phase-space-approach-to-m.tldr: Accounting for how many images share the same statistics clarifies Minimax Entropy learning and enables fast approximations.

paragraphs: This paper asks which sets of symbol sequences recurrent analog neural networks can recognize when noise affects every computational gate. The noise includes Gaussian noise and other common distributions whose probability density is nonzero over a large set. The question concerns the computational abilities that remain under these noise assumptions.

The authors give a precise characterization of the languages these networks can recognize. A striking consequence is that many regular languages fall outside that class. Their example is the set of binary strings that begin with zero: even this simple condition cannot be recognized by networks of the specified type. The result shows how strongly noise can constrain recurrent analog computation.

The paper also presents a construction method for feedforward analog networks that tolerate the same kinds of noise. Together, the results distinguish a limitation of the studied recurrent setting from the possibility of robust feedforward computation. They constrain designs for noise-resistant recurrent networks while also identifying a constructive route for a different network architecture.
neurips-1998-a-precise-characterization-.tldr: The paper characterizes language recognition under analog noise, finding severe recurrent-network restrictions alongside a robust feedforward construction.

paragraphs: This paper studies the expressive capacity of feedforward neural networks whose activation functions consist of polynomial pieces. It measures that capacity through VC dimension, which concerns how flexibly a model can assign binary labels to collections of inputs. The central question is how this capacity changes with the number of adjustable parameters.

The authors derive both upper and lower bounds. When the number of layers is fixed, the bounds establish growth proportional to W log W, where W counts the network parameters. Having bounds in both directions identifies the growth rate rather than merely placing a ceiling on what these networks can express.

The fixed-depth condition is essential to the comparison presented in the abstract. When the number of layers is unrestricted, the stated growth becomes quadratic in W. Thus, parameter count alone does not describe the capacity scaling: the permitted depth also matters. The result provides a theoretical distinction between increasing the size of a fixed-depth network and allowing depth to grow.
neurips-1998-almost-linear-vc-dimension-.tldr: For piecewise-polynomial networks, VC dimension grows as W log W at fixed depth, compared with quadratic growth when depth is unrestricted.

paragraphs: This paper translates a simplified Boundary Contour System into an analog chip architecture for real-time image processing. The design draws on models of several visual cortical cell types. Its purpose is to select image contours even when background clutter and noise make individual edge signals difficult to interpret.

Each pixel combines functions associated with simple, complex, hyper-complex, and bipole cells. These functions operate in three orientations, with pixels connected on a hexagonal grid. Analog current-mode CMOS circuits implement edge detection, local inhibition, direction-sensitive interactions over longer distances, and global gain control. The architecture therefore brings several stages of contour processing together within the pixel array.

The authors fabricated a prototype containing 12 by 10 pixels in 1.2-micrometer CMOS technology. Experiments with that prototype demonstrate robust contour selection against cluttered and noisy backgrounds. This provides hardware evidence for the proposed architecture: the coordinated processing is implemented in physical circuitry, and its contour-selection behavior is demonstrated on the fabricated device.
neurips-1998-analog-vlsi-cellular-implem.tldr: A fabricated analog chip implements cortical-inspired contour processing and demonstrates robustness to background clutter and noise.

paragraphs: This paper addresses reinforcement learning problems in which both the state space and time are continuous. The objective is to find optimal control through the value function, which describes the value associated with states. The authors focus on how to represent this function approximately while retaining a mathematical guarantee about learning.

Their representation uses a particular family of functions called barycentric interpolators. The key contribution is a set of sufficient conditions under which a reinforcement learning algorithm converges to the optimal value function. This ties the approximation method to a convergence result, giving a basis for determining when the representation can support the desired solution.

The guarantee also accommodates approximate models of state dynamics and reinforcement functions. Thus, the analysis addresses approximation in both the value representation and the descriptions of how the system behaves and supplies reinforcement. Its strength is conditional: satisfying the established conditions is enough for convergence, but the abstract does not claim that every use of barycentric interpolation or every approximate model will converge.
neurips-1998-barycentric-interpolators-f.tldr: Barycentric value-function approximations support conditional convergence guarantees for continuous-time, continuous-state reinforcement learning, even with approximate models.

paragraphs: This paper develops a faster implementation of probabilistic image matching for face recognition and image retrieval. The underlying method evaluates similarity through a Bayesian analysis of differences between images. Earlier work used this analysis to build a dual representation related to eigenfaces, providing a probabilistic basis for deciding how closely two faces match.

The abstract reports that the earlier matching algorithm outperformed standard Euclidean nearest-neighbor eigenface matching and was the top performer in the cited face-recognition competition. That finding motivates making the probabilistic method cheaper to use. The new development targets the computational expense of evaluating nonlinear Bayesian similarity measures during matching.

The proposed replacement uses linear subspace projections computed offline and simple Euclidean norms computed online. This shifts the work into a form that reduces the cost of individual comparisons. The authors report a significant computational speedup, making the approach more practical for very large image databases. The contribution is therefore a more efficient realization of an already demonstrated probabilistic matching approach.
neurips-1998-bayesian-modeling-of-facial.tldr: Offline linear projections and simple online distances substantially speed up Bayesian face matching for large image databases.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how people learn a concept from only a few examples that belong to it. It combines theoretical analysis with a human-subject study using concepts represented as axis-aligned rectangles in a multidimensional feature space. This simple setting makes it possible to examine how learners extend a concept beyond the examples they have seen.

The author reports that existing learning models, when applied to this task, cannot explain the subjects' generalization from small samples. The proposed Bayesian model rests on a specific assumption: the examples are sampled randomly from the concept being learned. The sampling process therefore becomes part of the explanation for how examples support different possible concepts.

The model closely fits human behavior on the rectangle task. The paper also uses it to offer qualitative insights into more realistic forms of concept learning. These are different levels of support: precise behavioral fits are reported for the simple task, while the broader cases receive qualitative interpretation. The work connects a probabilistic account of examples to observed human generalization.
neurips-1998-bayesian-modeling-of-human-.tldr: A Bayesian model assuming random positive examples closely explains human generalization in a simple concept-learning task.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis (PCA) represents data using a reduced set of components. The number retained sets the dimensionality of that representation. This paper builds on a probabilistic formulation in which PCA arises as the maximum likelihood solution of a generative model with latent variables: unobserved quantities used to explain the observed data.

The paper uses that formulation as the starting point for a Bayesian treatment. Its central result is that Bayesian inference can determine the effective dimensionality of the latent space automatically. In PCA terms, this means that deciding how many principal components to retain can become part of the inference procedure itself. The approach therefore brings the choice of representation size into the same framework used to infer the model.

The abstract also highlights mixtures of probabilistic PCA models as an application. In such a mixture, each component can determine its own effective complexity. This permits different components within a single mixture to use different effective dimensionalities, allowing complexity to be determined separately for each component.
neurips-1998-bayesian-pca-819625bf83.tldr: Bayesian PCA can automatically determine how many principal components to retain, including a separate effective dimensionality for each component of a probabilistic PCA mixture.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a method for recovering sources from multiple observed channels when the sources have been mixed and filtered. Its central modeling assumption is that both the mixing process and the system used to undo it can be described by stable linear state-space systems. This provides a common representation for the original transformation and its reversal.

The method divides the task into source separation and state estimation. For separation, the authors derive a learning algorithm that adjusts the matrices in the output equation by minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence. For state estimation, they introduce a quantity called hidden innovation to support a numerical implementation of the Kalman filter.

This division lets the method address the output mapping and the internal state of the demixing model as distinct parts of one procedure. The authors report computer simulations demonstrating the validity and high effectiveness of the state-space approach. The evidence supports the proposed combination within the studied setup, whose formulation depends on the stable linear models specified at the outset.
neurips-1998-blind-separation-of-filtere.tldr: A stable linear state-space formulation separates filtered sources by combining divergence-based learning with Kalman state estimation.

paragraphs: This paper combines two approaches to classification that offer complementary strengths. Generative probability models, including hidden Markov models, provide a principled treatment of missing information and sequences of different lengths. Discriminative methods, including support vector machines, offer flexible decision boundaries and often achieve better classification performance than model-based approaches.

The proposed connection is to derive kernel functions from generative probability models and use those kernels within discriminative classifiers. A kernel supplies the comparison that the discriminative method uses between inputs. Deriving it from a generative model allows information captured by that model to contribute to the classification decision.

The authors provide a theoretical justification for this combination and demonstrate a substantial classification improvement in DNA and protein sequence analysis. These results support the usefulness of combining structured probabilistic modeling with discriminative learning in the sequence-analysis setting studied. The contribution is a concrete interface between the two approaches: the generative model supplies the kernel through which the discriminative classifier works.
neurips-1998-exploiting-generative-model.tldr: Kernels derived from generative models connect probabilistic sequence modeling to discriminative classifiers and improve DNA and protein classification.

paragraphs: This paper develops mathematical bounds on several kinds of Bayesian prediction error in Gaussian-process regression. The aim is to characterize prediction error through inequalities that constrain its possible size. A simple convexity lemma provides the starting point for deriving these results across the error measures considered.

The basic bounds apply to a fixed training set. This makes the actual collection of training examples the starting point of the analysis. The authors then obtain simpler expressions under an additional sampling condition: the distribution used to draw inputs equals the weight function associated with the covariance kernel. That relationship is part of the setting for the simplified results.

Under this sampling setup, the resulting bounds are asymptotically tight, meaning they approach the error behavior they are intended to describe in the relevant limit. The authors also compare their results with numerical experiments. The paper thus connects a general fixed-training-set analysis with simpler, tight asymptotic expressions available under the stated relationship between sampling and kernel weighting.
neurips-1998-general-bounds-on-bayes-err.tldr: Convexity-based bounds characterize Gaussian-process regression errors, with simpler asymptotically tight results under a specified sampling condition.

paragraphs: This paper proposes identifying texture through how economically an image region can be described. A region counts as texture when its statistics provide a more compact description than the exact arrangement of its parts. This working definition turns texture detection into a question about local regularity and departures from that regularity.

The method looks for points that are unusual relative to local statistics. Regions without such outliers receive texture labels. At the same time, the unusual points provide low-level, bottom-up cues for visual attention. The authors connect this approach to psychophysical findings about texture processing and visual popout, bringing the two kinds of labeling into one method.

The motivation is that image-processing systems often need to treat objects and texture differently but require a way to determine which regions belong to each. The supplied text also emphasizes that this distinction can depend on scale. The proposed statistical criterion supplies a practical way to label natural scenes while acknowledging that texture is a characterization made at a particular scale of interest.
neurips-1998-general-purpose-localizatio.tldr: A local-statistics method labels texture where outliers are absent and uses outliers as cues for visual attention.

paragraphs: This paper investigates a generative model for binary observations that uses a small number of continuous hidden units. The model connects a compact continuous representation to outputs with only two possible values. Its design includes a clipping nonlinearity, which distinguishes the relationship between hidden variables and outputs from conventional principal component analysis.

Learning relies on the relationship between correlations among underlying continuous Gaussian variables and correlations among the resulting binary variables. The authors use those relationships to determine the network's weights. This gives the learning procedure a way to connect observable binary dependencies to the continuous structure assumed by the model.

The advantages of the approach are illustrated with a translationally invariant binary distribution and handwritten digit images. These examples show its application to both a specified binary distribution and image data. The central contribution is the combination of continuous hidden variables, nonlinear binary outputs, and correlation-based weight learning. Together, these elements provide a generative representation tailored to binary observations while retaining a small continuous hidden space.
neurips-1998-learning-a-continuous-hidde.tldr: A compact continuous latent model learns binary data by relating Gaussian-variable correlations to correlations after nonlinear clipping.

paragraphs: This paper makes template-based classification insensitive to rotations within the image plane by handling orientation before classification. The training images contain upright examples. The method uses those examples to generate candidate orientations of an input, allowing the later classifier to work with the upright views it was trained to recognize.

Orientation is estimated separately under each possible class hypothesis. For a given class, the input image is rotated to maximize similarity to that class's training images. Repeating this process produces several candidate images. The paper states that at least one of these views places the object upright, after which models trained only on upright examples can classify the candidates.

The authors report successful applications to rotated handwritten digit recognition and rotated face detection in cluttered scenes. The approach matters because it gives orientation discrimination an explicit role before the final recognition decision. Its class-dependent alignment procedure provides a simple, efficient route for using upright templates when the objects presented at recognition time may have arbitrary in-plane rotations.
neurips-1998-making-templates-rotational.tldr: Class-specific rotation alignment lets classifiers trained on upright examples recognize rotated digits and detect rotated faces.

paragraphs: This paper extends expectation maximization to conditional density estimation when data are missing. The distinction concerns the objective being optimized. Ordinary EM targets joint likelihood, while the proposed Conditional Expectation Maximization algorithm targets conditional likelihood: the probability of the quantities to be predicted given the quantities available as conditions.

The authors construct a bounding-and-maximization procedure specifically for that conditional objective. They apply it to conditioned mixture models and derive parameter update rules using the bounds. This supplies an optimization method aligned with conditional prediction while retaining the iterative structure of improving a bound and updating the model.

The paper demonstrates monotonic convergence, computational efficiency, and regression results superior to EM in the comparisons reported. Monotonic convergence describes the behavior of the optimization procedure; the regression comparison describes the observed predictive results. Together, these findings support adapting the fitting objective to the conditional task. The contribution is both an extension of EM for missing-data settings and a concrete set of updates for conditioned mixture models.
neurips-1998-maximum-conditional-likelih.tldr: Conditional EM optimizes conditional likelihood through bound maximization and demonstrates monotonic convergence and improved regression results over EM.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to set a classifier's decision threshold when the training classes are imbalanced. Its theoretical starting point is prior work connecting large classification margins with generalization through the fat-shattering dimension. The authors examine what those results imply when the available examples are distributed unevenly across classes.

They develop two approaches to choosing the threshold and incorporate them into ThetaBoost. ThetaBoost is a boosting algorithm designed to handle unequal loss functions, so different kinds of mistakes can carry different consequences. Threshold selection is therefore considered alongside both class imbalance and the losses attached to classification decisions.

The authors experimentally test ThetaBoost and the two threshold-setting approaches. The supplied abstract establishes that this evaluation was performed without stating a particular performance advantage. The contribution is the development and testing of threshold-selection methods motivated by margin-based learning theory. It brings the question of where to place the decision cutoff into a framework that explicitly accommodates unequal losses and examines the implications of imbalanced training data.
neurips-1998-optimizing-classifers-for-i.tldr: The paper develops and tests two margin-theory-based threshold-setting approaches within ThetaBoost for imbalanced data and unequal losses.

paragraphs: This paper develops consequences of an equivalence between Adaptive Ridge regression and Lasso. Adaptive Ridge balances a separate quadratic penalty on each model parameter. The equivalence is stated at the level of the resulting estimate: the two procedures produce the same estimate, allowing Lasso to be viewed through a particular adaptive quadratic-penalty formulation.

The authors use that connection to derive a fixed-point algorithm for computing the Lasso solution. The alternative formulation therefore has a practical role in designing a solver. The analogy also supplies a new hyperparameter for controlling model complexity, offering another way to tune the balance between fitting the data and restricting the model.

The paper then presents possible extensions of Lasso-style sparse regression to kernel smoothing, additive modeling, and neural-network training. These extensions are proposed possibilities, while the fixed-point algorithm follows from the stated equivalence. The broader significance is that a connection between two penalty formulations can generate both a computational method and new directions for applying sparse estimation.
neurips-1998-outcomes-of-the-equivalence.tldr: The equivalence of Adaptive Ridge and Lasso yields a fixed-point solver, a complexity-control hyperparameter, and possible sparse-modeling extensions.

paragraphs: This paper revisits the spiral benchmark as a problem of perceptual organization that can be approached without learning. The authors connect it to determining inside/outside relationships. That connection motivates a common solution based on how activity in a network coordinates over time, rather than on training the network to classify examples.

The proposed mechanism uses oscillatory correlation in a network with time delays. Its simulation results agree qualitatively with human performance. The authors interpret human limitations through synchronization and delays, treating these as biologically plausible ingredients. The agreement supports their proposed interpretation at a qualitative level rather than establishing a precise behavioral fit.

A special version of the network removes the time delays. The authors state that this version can always distinguish the figures in question regardless of shape, position, size, or orientation. The contrast between delayed and delay-free versions gives timing a central explanatory role: the same general mechanism can express perceptual limitations with delays and unrestricted discrimination of these figures in the stated special case.
neurips-1998-perceiving-without-learning.tldr: An oscillatory network connects spiral discrimination with inside/outside perception, using time delays to interpret qualitative human limitations.

paragraphs: This paper examines how recurrent circuitry could produce the spatial-phase invariance associated with complex cells in visual cortex. Spatial-phase invariance means a response is less sensitive to the precise spatial alignment of the input pattern. The authors propose that recurrent amplification of feedforward input can generate this property within a network model.

The key observation is that amplification can broaden selectivity as well as sharpen it. In the proposed network, neurons show simple-cell-like responses at low gain and complex-cell-like responses at high gain. Changing the strength of amplification therefore changes the response pattern expressed by the modeled neurons, connecting the two behaviors through the same recurrent mechanism.

The finding gives recurrent amplification a possible role in generating invariance, alongside its proposed role in enhancing selectivity. The authors also suggest that similar mechanisms may contribute to invariant representations elsewhere in visual processing. That broader application remains a possibility; the concrete result described here is the gain-dependent transition between simple- and complex-cell-like responses in the network model.
neurips-1998-recurrent-cortical-amplific.tldr: A recurrent visual-cortex model shifts from simple-cell-like to complex-cell-like responses as amplification gain increases.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a support vector machine that learns from labeled examples together with a specified set of unlabeled points. Its goal is transduction: predicting labels for those particular points. This differs from first learning a general classification function and then applying that fixed function to whatever inputs later require predictions.

The proposed model balances misclassification error with function capacity using all the available data. For linear support vector machines with a 1-norm formulation, the authors show how to express the problem as a mixed-integer program. Integer programming then provides a way to solve that formulation exactly, connecting the learning objective to a concrete optimization method.

The authors compare the method with a conventional 1-norm support vector machine on ten datasets. In each comparison, generalization either improves or shows no significant difference. They interpret these results as supporting the value of including unlabeled working data when labeled training information is insufficient. The finding is empirical support in the tested cases, with the motivating benefit tied to limited training information.
neurips-1998-semi-supervised-support-vec.tldr: A transductive support vector machine uses unlabeled working data and matches or improves generalization across ten tested datasets.

paragraphs: This paper links network regularization with independent component analysis by showing that a particular complexity-reduction method can extract independent features as a by-product. The method is Flat Minimum Search, which minimizes training error together with the precision needed to specify network weights. The claim concerns this demonstrated representative of a broader class of regularizers.

The theoretical analysis examines an autoassociator trained with Flat Minimum Search. It indicates that the hidden layer attempts to represent each input through a sparse code using as few simple features as possible. This connects pressure for a low-complexity network with the emergence of a compact representation of the input's underlying sources.

In experiments, the method finds optimal codes on difficult versions of the noisy-bars problem by separating sources, while ICA and PCA fail on those cases. For real-world images, it uses fewer bits per pixel than ICA or PCA. These findings show that the studied regularization procedure can support both source separation and efficient coding, without establishing that all complexity-reducing methods do so.
neurips-1998-source-separation-as-a-by-p.tldr: Flat Minimum Search can produce sparse, source-separating representations as a by-product of reducing network complexity.

paragraphs: This paper proposes randomized GACV, a method for choosing smoothing or bandwidth parameters in probabilistic binary classification. Here the learner estimates the probability of class membership for a given input. The tuning problem is to balance close agreement with the observed data against the complexity of the fitted probability function.

The target is Kullback-Leibler distance between the estimated probability distribution and the true population distribution. This makes the quality of the probability estimates central to parameter selection. The method uses an in-sample approximation to cross-validation to guide that choice, connecting the fit-complexity tradeoff to the population-level probability target.

Its computational device is a randomized estimate of the trace of a Hessian, a quantity describing aspects of the fitted objective's curvature. The procedure mimics cross-validation using a single additional learning run with perturbed outcomes. The contribution is therefore a way to approximate a validation-based tuning calculation at the cost of that one relearning step, while directing the choice toward the stated distributional objective.
neurips-1998-the-bias-variance-tradeoff-.tldr: Randomized GACV tunes probabilistic classifiers by approximating cross-validation with one relearning step on perturbed outcomes.

paragraphs: This paper studies how competition between neurons affects the development of visual maps and preferences for one eye. The model allows competition strength to vary. With weak competition it resembles correlation-based learning; with strong competition it becomes a self-organizing map. This provides a way to examine different developmental behaviors within one model.

The change in competition also changes which input properties shape receptive fields. Weak competition emphasizes second-order statistics, while stronger competition brings higher moments and features of individual patterns into play. For correlated, localized inputs from both eyes, a topographic map and localized binocular receptive fields appear after competition exceeds one critical level. Eye dominance appears beyond a second critical level.

Anti-correlated activity between the eyes produces a different sequence. Second-order statistics can drive eye dominance even under weak competition, but topographic organization still requires competition beyond a critical level. The results distinguish eye preference from spatial map formation: their emergence depends differently on input correlations and competition strength in the studied developmental model.
neurips-1998-the-role-of-lateral-cortica.tldr: A developmental model shows that lateral competition and inter-eye correlations jointly shape topographic organization and eye dominance.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an unsupervised classification method based on a mixture of independent component analysis models. It assumes that observations belong to mutually exclusive classes and that each class is generated by a linear mixture of independent sources. Each class can therefore have its own source structure and mixing relationship.

The algorithm learns the independent sources and mixing matrix for every class, while also assigning each observation a probability of membership in each class. It extends Gaussian mixture modeling by allowing non-Gaussian structure within classes. The method combines uncertainty about class membership with a separate learned representation for the data assigned to each class.

The authors demonstrate efficient image codes for natural scenes and text. They report that the learned classes of basis functions better approximate the underlying data distributions and can consequently improve coding efficiency. They also suggest broader potential for modeling high-dimensional structure. The demonstrated contribution is the use of multiple ICA representations to capture different kinds of structure within one probabilistic classification and coding framework.
neurips-1998-unsupervised-classification.tldr: An ICA mixture model learns non-Gaussian classes, source representations, and membership probabilities, with demonstrated applications to efficient image coding.

paragraphs: This paper presents the Generalization Learning System, a hybrid classifier system designed to address credit assignment and the mismatch between individual rule strength and overall rule-set performance. The authors frame classifier systems as model-free learning in partially observable Markov decision processes. This places rule selection and rule-set behavior within a policy-learning perspective.

The system divides its search between choosing rule conditions and improving behavior under those conditions. Given a fixed set of rule conditions, it uses a policy-improvement procedure aimed at a locally optimal stochastic policy. A genetic algorithm searches for the set of rule conditions, with the total number of rules held fixed.

This division gives the two searches different responsibilities: one improves the policy for an existing description of situations, while the other changes that description to seek better generalization. The design aims to address the identified classifier-system problems through this combination. Its stated local policy objective should be distinguished from the broader search for the best rule conditions; the abstract does not assert a global optimum for the combined system.
neurips-1998-viewing-classifier-systems-.tldr: GLS combines local stochastic-policy improvement with genetic search over rule conditions in a model-free POMDP framework.
